The dual-branch student processes the tile in parallel: a Visual Branch (ResNet-18) captures global tissue appearance, and a Graph Branch builds and encodes a microenvironment graph from NuLite segmentations. The fused features are optimised to match the teacher embedding. 3.1 Overall Distillation Framework As illustrated in Fig. 1 , G-Interp distils representations from a frozen PFM teacher into a lightweight dual-branch student. Given an image tile 𝐗 \mathbf{X} , the teacher outputs a high-dimensional embedding 𝐞 T ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{e}_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , and the student produces a corresponding embedding 𝐞 S ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{e}_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . Cell Segmentation and Feature Extraction. We employ NuLite for nucleus instance segmentation and type classification.

For each detected cell i i , we form a 51D node feature 𝐡 i ( 0 ) \mathbf{h}_{i}^{(0)} by concatenating: (a) 37 morphology descriptors (e.g., region properties, Hu moments, and shape/boundary features, augmented with within-patch statistics), (b) a 6D one-hot vector of the predicted nucleus type, and (c) an 8D sinusoidal positional encoding of the centroid coordinates. 2. Graph Construction. We build a patch-level undirected cell graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) using nucleus centroids as spatial anchors. To reduce boundary artefacts, we discard nuclei near the patch border and mark patches with fewer than 5 remaining cells as invalid. We then construct a k k -NN graph ( k = 5 k=5 ) by Euclidean centroid distance. Each edge ( i , j ) (i,j) is assigned an 18D attribute comprising a 16-kernel RBF embedding of inter-cell distance (cut-off 200 pixels) and a 2D unit direction vector from j j to i i . 3. Graph Representation Learning. We embed node and edge attributes into a shared 512D hidden space using lightweight MLP encoders, and apply a GNN backbone (GATv2 [ 3 ] , TransformerConv [ 23 ] , or SAGPool [ 28 ] ). We aggregate node embeddings into a graph-level representation via attentional readout (attention-based backbones) or hierarchical pooling (SAGPool), and map it with a projection head to obtain the graph embedding 𝐯 g ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{v}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . 4. Attention-based evidence extraction. For attention-based backbones (GATv2 [ 3 ] and TransformerConv [ 23 ] ), we take edge attention as the last-layer attention coefficients α i ​ j \alpha_{ij} (averaged over heads) and derive node attention by aggregating incident α i ​ j \alpha_{ij} and normalising within each patch. For SAGPool [ 28 ] , we use the pooling scores as node importance, but cannot report edge attentions. 3.3 Visual Branch and Dual-branch Fusion Strategies Visual Feature Extraction.

ResNet-18 backbone processes the raw tile and produces a visual embedding 𝐯 v ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{v}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} to complement GNN with tissue context. Fusion Strategies. We fuse 𝐯 g \mathbf{v}_{g} and 𝐯 v \mathbf{v}_{v} to synergise cellular and contextual representations. In our implementation (and as summarised in Fig. 1 ), we consider three lightweight fusion modules: 1. Concatenation Fusion (Concat). We can concatenate the two embeddings and pass them through an MLP layer, as follows: 𝐞 S = MLP cat ( [ 𝐯 v | | 𝐯 g ] ) . \mathbf{e}_{S}=\mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{cat}}\big([\mathbf{v}_{v}\,||\,\mathbf{v}_{g}]\big). (2) 2. Gated Fusion (Gate). We concatenate the embeddings and predict an element-wise gate 𝝀 ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) D \boldsymbol{\lambda}\in(0,1)^{D} to balance the two branches: 𝝀 = σ ( MLP gate ( [ 𝐯 v | | 𝐯 g ] ) ) , 𝐡 = 𝝀 ⊙ 𝐯 v + ( 1 − 𝝀 ) ⊙ 𝐯 g , 𝐞 S = MLP out ( 𝐡 ) . \boldsymbol{\lambda}=\sigma\!\left(\mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{gate}}([\mathbf{v}_{v}\,||\,\mathbf{v}_{g}])\right),\quad\mathbf{h}=\boldsymbol{\lambda}\odot\mathbf{v}_{v}+(1-\boldsymbol{\lambda})\odot\mathbf{v}_{g},\quad\mathbf{e}_{S}=\mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{h}). (3) Here, | | || denotes concatenation, and ⊙ \odot denotes the Hadamard product. 3. Cross-Attention Interaction (Attn). As illustrated in Fig. 1 ("Cross-attention interaction"), we retain patch-level image tokens from the visual encoder and use cell node embeddings to query them. Concretely, for each cell node embedding 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} , we perform cross-attention with node queries and token keys/values, and update the node representation with a residual connection: 𝐡 i ← 𝐡 i + CrossAttn ​ ( q = 𝐡 i , k = v = 𝐓 ) , \mathbf{h}_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}_{i}+\mathrm{CrossAttn}(q=\mathbf{h}_{i},\;k=v=\mathbf{T}), (4) where 𝐓 \mathbf{T} denotes the ResNet patch tokens.

This allows each cell node to explicitly “read” visual evidence from its corresponding tile, improving distillation capacity and aligning graph-based explanations with the visual context. 3.2 Graph Branch: Microenvironmental Modelling The graph branch captures cellular-level microenvironmental features as: 1. We evaluate generalisation on three external cohorts: Yale-HER2 [ 9 , 8 ] ( n = 192 n=192 ), SLN-Breast [ 5 , 6 ] ( n = 130 n=130 ), and BRACS [ 2 ] ( n = 547 n=547 ). All slides are tiled at 20 × \times into 256 × 256 256\times 256 patches. Yale-HER2 and SLN-Breast are binary classification benchmarks, while BRACS is a 7-class classification task. For distillation, we sample cell-containing tiles and split them into 90% training and 10% validation. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW (lr 5 × 10 − 4 5{\times}10^{-4} , wd 1 × 10 − 5 1{\times}10^{-5} ) and a 1-epoch linear warm-up, using a total batch size of 512 across four A800 GPUs; each epoch sub-samples 20% of training tiles, and we select the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. For downstream WSI classification, we extract frozen student tile embeddings and train an attention-based MIL aggregator (ABMIL [ 15 ] ) for 20 epochs (lr 1 × 10 − 4 1{\times}10^{-4} ) with 5-fold cross-validation, using final-epoch weights per fold for evaluation.

4.2 Predictive Performance Evaluation We compare G-Interp with PFM teachers and the single-branch ResNet-18 KD baseline (Vanilla KD) across the three cohorts (Table 1 ). G-Interp consistently improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) over the single-branch baseline, including on BRACS (7-class classification). Despite reducing the parameter count by over 20 × 20\times , it matches or exceeds the teacher in settings, indicating that explicit microenvironment modelling can regularise distillation and suppress task-irrelevant variation in teacher embeddings. Across fusion variants, no single mechanism is consistently dominant. 4.3 Interpretability and Biological Faithfulness Beyond predictive performance, G-Interp provides microenvironmental interpretability by revealing cell- and interaction-level evidence for PFM decisions. We assess whether the student highlights biologically meaningful evidence, focusing on: (1) cellular faithfulness, (2) adaptive gate behaviour, and (3) microenvironment interaction patterns. Qualitative visualisations use the GATv2+Gate student on Yale-HER2. Cellular Faithfulness and Visual Refinement. We test whether high-attention cells identified by the graph branch are causally important by synchronising occlusions across both branches and re-measuring similarity to the frozen teacher. As shown in Fig. 2 (A), occluding Top- k k cells (highest GAT attention) consistently causes a larger drop in cosine similarity of the tile embeddings than occluding Bottom- k k or random cells, across all three teachers. We visualise the corresponding salient nodes and edges in Fig. 2 (C). We further examine whether joint distillation refines the visual encoder. Layer-1 Score-CAM maps (Fig. 2 B) show that the dual-branch student concentrates activation around nuclei more tightly than the ImageNet-pretrained and single-branch KD baselines, suggesting that the graph prior suppresses background responses.

Adaptive Gating Mechanism. We analyse how the gate value λ \lambda controls the relative contribution of the two branches, where low λ \lambda emphasises the graph embedding and high λ \lambda emphasises the visual embedding. Fig. 3 (A) shows that λ \lambda spans a wide range across tiles, indicating that the model does not use a fixed mixing ratio but adjusts the fusion weights across samples. Example tiles (Fig. 3 (B)) suggest that low λ \lambda is often associated with cell-dense regions with richer local interactions, whereas high λ \lambda tends to occur in cell-sparse background regions (e.g., stroma/adipose). Microenvironment Interaction Patterns. We aggregate the top 10% highest-attention edges to form class-wise cell–cell communication heatmaps (Fig. 3 (C)). Here, same-type interactions refer to edges linking two cells of the same predicted type, while cross-type interactions link different cell types. While same-type interactions are overall dominant, the Positive class shows relatively stronger cross-type connectivity. Notably, the Virchow2-distilled model exhibits comparatively increased cross-type interactions even in the Negative class, suggesting a stronger preference for diverse inter-cellular relations. To quantify spatial patterns, we relate neoplastic-cell attention to the distance from the tumour–stroma boundary (Fig. 3 (D)). Across teachers, attention is higher for cells deeper within tumour nests; compared with UNI v2 and Phikon v2, Virchow2 shows a flatter decay with distance, indicating a weaker contrast between boundary-adjacent and deep-tumour neoplastic cells. 4.1 Datasets and Experimental Details We perform self-supervised distillation pre-training on TCGA-BRCA ( n = 1 , 133 n=1{,}133 slides from 40 sites). Across fusion variants, no single mechanism is consistently dominant. 5 Conclusion We presented G-Interp , a graph-visual distillation framework that adapts frozen pathology foundation models into lightweight students while providing cellular- and interaction-level evidence. By distilling teacher embeddings into a dual-branch student with a microenvironment graph interpreter and adaptive fusion, G-Interp achieves strong performance across three external breast cancer cohorts.

Beyond AUC, we showed that graph attention supports faithful cell-level attribution, the gating mechanism responds to tissue content, and the distilled students reveal teacher-specific microenvironmental preferences in how attention varies across cell types and spatial contexts. These results position G-Interp as a practical route to efficient deployment and a tool for analysing how PFMs encode microenvironmental signals. Future work will extend G-Interp to broader cancer types and evaluate robustness under varied staining and scanning conditions. {credits} 5.0.1 Acknowledgements This work was supported by the following grants.
